subject: Reproductive
vignette: A 42-year-old woman presents with heavy menstrual bleeding and progressively severe pelvic pain during menses. Pelvic examination shows a diffusely enlarged, globular, soft ('boggy') uterus. Ultrasound reveals small cystic spaces within the myometrium.
question: Which of the following best explains this patient's findings?

options.text: Endometrial tissue implanted on the pelvic peritoneum
Endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium
Fibrous bands within the endometrial cavity
Proliferation of atypical endometrial glands from unopposed estrogen
A well-circumscribed whorled smooth muscle tumor

explanation_correct: Adenomyosis is defined by the presence of endometrial tissue (glands and stroma) within the myometrium, thought to arise from invagination of the basal layer of the endometrium or metaplasia of remnant progenitor cells. It presents with abnormal uterine bleeding and dysmenorrhea. The uterus is characteristically diffusely enlarged ('globular') and soft ('boggy') on examination, distinguishing it from the nodular contour of discrete leiomyomas.

explanation_incorrect.A: Endometriosis is endometrial tissue outside the uterus (eg, peritoneum, ovaries), not within the myometrium, and the uterus is usually normal-sized on exam.
explanation_incorrect.C: Intrauterine (Asherman) adhesions are fibrous bands in the endometrial cavity that cause decreased menses and infertility, typically after dilation and curettage, not a boggy enlarged uterus.
explanation_incorrect.D: Endometrial hyperplasia is abnormal gland proliferation from unopposed estrogen and does not produce a diffusely enlarged boggy uterus with intramyometrial tissue.
explanation_incorrect.E: Leiomyoma is a benign myometrial tumor that produces a nodular, irregularly enlarged uterus on exam rather than a diffuse globular boggy enlargement.

educationalObjective: Adenomyosis is endometrial tissue within the myometrium causing dysmenorrhea and a diffusely enlarged, boggy uterus.

subject: Reproductive
vignette: A 30-year-old woman has progressive dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and infertility. Pelvic examination is largely normal but notes slight tenderness and nodularity of the uterosacral ligaments. Laparoscopy reveals yellow-brown 'powder burn' implants on the pelvic peritoneum and a blood-filled ovarian cyst.
question: Which of the following best describes the pathogenesis of this patient's condition?

options.text: Invagination of the basal endometrium into the myometrium
Unopposed estrogen stimulation of endometrial glands
Direct inoculation of the uterine cavity by vaginal flora after delivery
Ectopic implantation of endometrial tissue via retrograde menstruation
Fibrous band formation after curettage trauma

explanation_correct: Endometriosis is the presence of endometrial tissue (glands and stroma) outside the uterus. A leading theory is ectopic implantation of shed endometrial cells via retrograde menstruation through the fallopian tubes (also via lymphatics or blood vessels); metaplasia of remnant progenitor cells is another theory. Implants on the ovaries can enlarge into blood-filled 'chocolate' cysts (endometriomas). It causes dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, infertility, and abnormal bleeding, though the physical exam is often normal.

explanation_incorrect.A: Invagination of basal endometrium into the myometrium describes adenomyosis, which is confined to the uterine wall rather than producing extra-uterine powder-burn implants.
explanation_incorrect.B: Unopposed estrogen causing glandular proliferation describes endometrial hyperplasia, which presents with abnormal bleeding rather than extra-uterine implants and chocolate cysts.
explanation_incorrect.C: Inoculation of the uterine cavity by vaginal microbiota after delivery describes endometritis, which presents with fever, uterine tenderness, and purulent lochia.
explanation_incorrect.E: Fibrous bands after curettage describe intrauterine adhesions (Asherman syndrome), which reduce menses and cause infertility, not extra-uterine endometrial implants.

educationalObjective: Endometriosis is ectopic endometrial tissue outside the uterus, sown by retrograde menses, forming powder-burn peritoneal lesions and chocolate cysts.

subject: Reproductive
vignette: A 55-year-old woman with obesity and chronic anovulation due to PCOS presents with abnormal uterine bleeding. Endometrial biopsy shows an increased number of crowded endometrial glands. Her physician is concerned about progression to carcinoma.
question: Which of the following best describes the mechanism driving this endometrial proliferation?

options.text: Excess estrogen unopposed by progesterone
Elevated progesterone from a corpus luteum cyst
Androgen excess converted to dihydrotestosterone
Chronic endometrial inflammation from polymicrobial infection
Mechanical trauma to the basalis layer from dilation and curettage

explanation_correct: Endometrial hyperplasia is abnormal proliferation of endometrial glands caused by excess estrogen that is unopposed by progesterone. Progesterone normally limits endometrial growth, so chronic anovulation (no corpus luteum progesterone), obesity, nulliparity, HRT, and tamoxifen all predispose. It presents with abnormal uterine bleeding and conveys an increased risk of endometrial carcinoma, especially when nuclear atypia is present.

explanation_incorrect.B: Progesterone opposes estrogen-driven endometrial proliferation and is protective; a progesterone-secreting state would not cause hyperplasia.
explanation_incorrect.C: Androgen excess with conversion to DHT relates to hirsutism and acne, not the endometrial gland proliferation of hyperplasia.
explanation_incorrect.D: Polymicrobial infection of the endometrium after delivery causes endometritis (fever, uterine tenderness, purulent lochia), not hyperplasia.
explanation_incorrect.E: Trauma to the basalis layer from dilation and curettage causes intrauterine adhesions (Asherman syndrome), not glandular hyperplasia.

educationalObjective: Endometrial hyperplasia results from unopposed estrogen (obesity, anovulation/PCOS, nulliparity, HRT, tamoxifen) and raises carcinoma risk, especially with nuclear atypia.

subject: Reproductive
vignette: A 28-year-old woman develops fever, uterine tenderness, and purulent lochia 3 days after delivery. She delivered by cesarean section.
question: Which of the following is the most important risk factor for this patient's condition?

options.text: Retained products of conception after a vaginal delivery
Breastfeeding
Cesarean section
Early ambulation after delivery
Use of intrauterine contraception years earlier

explanation_correct: Endometritis is inflammation of the endometrium, usually occurring after delivery from inoculation of the uterine cavity by vaginal microbiota. Cesarean section is the most important risk factor because sutures and necrotic tissue act as a nidus for polymicrobial infection. It presents with fever, uterine tenderness, and purulent lochia.

explanation_incorrect.A: Retained products can contribute to postpartum infection, but cesarean section with its sutures and necrotic tissue is the single most important risk factor.
explanation_incorrect.B: Breastfeeding is protective and does not predispose to endometritis; it promotes uterine involution.
explanation_incorrect.D: Early ambulation reduces thrombotic risk and is not a risk factor for endometritis.
explanation_incorrect.E: Prior intrauterine contraception is not the major risk factor for postpartum endometritis; the key risk is cesarean delivery.

educationalObjective: Postpartum endometritis is polymicrobial, and cesarean section is the most important risk factor due to sutures and necrotic tissue acting as a nidus.

subject: Reproductive
vignette: A 34-year-old woman has had multiple dilation and curettage procedures following miscarriages. She now reports markedly decreased menstrual flow, infertility, and dysmenorrhea. Hysteroscopy shows fibrous bands crossing the endometrial cavity.
question: Which of the following best explains this patient's findings?

options.text: Endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium
Ectopic endometrial implants on the ovaries
Confluent endometrial glands without intervening stroma
Whorled bundles of smooth muscle in the myometrium
Fibrous adhesions within the endometrial cavity from basalis injury

explanation_correct: Intrauterine adhesions are fibrous bands within the endometrial cavity caused by damage to the basalis layer of the endometrium, most often after dilation and curettage. When symptomatic they are called Asherman syndrome. They present with decreased menses, infertility, recurrent pregnancy loss, and dysmenorrhea.

explanation_incorrect.A: Endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium is adenomyosis, which causes a boggy enlarged uterus and dysmenorrhea, not intrauterine fibrous bands with decreased menses.
explanation_incorrect.B: Ectopic endometrial implants on the ovaries are endometriosis, which causes chocolate cysts and infertility but not intrauterine adhesions.
explanation_incorrect.C: Confluent glands without intervening stroma is the histology of endometrioid carcinoma, an endometrial malignancy, not Asherman syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.D: Whorled smooth muscle bundles describe a leiomyoma (fibroid), a myometrial tumor, not fibrous bands within the cavity.

educationalObjective: Asherman syndrome is intrauterine adhesions from basalis injury (classically after D&C) causing hypomenorrhea, infertility, and recurrent pregnancy loss.

subject: Reproductive
vignette: Two patients are being compared. Patient 1 has a diffusely enlarged, boggy uterus with endometrial tissue found within the myometrium on hysterectomy. Patient 2 has a normal-sized uterus, powder-burn peritoneal lesions, and ovarian chocolate cysts.
question: Which of the following statements regarding these two conditions is correct?

options.text: Both are characterized by confluent endometrial glands without intervening stroma
Both arise from unopposed estrogen and carry high malignant potential
Patient 1 has adenomyosis, whereas patient 2 has endometriosis
Patient 1 has endometriosis, whereas patient 2 has adenomyosis
Both are inflammatory processes triggered by polymicrobial infection after cesarean delivery

explanation_correct: Adenomyosis is endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium, producing a diffusely enlarged, globular, boggy uterus and dysmenorrhea. Endometriosis is endometrial tissue outside the uterus, sown by retrograde menses, producing powder-burn peritoneal implants and ovarian endometriomas (chocolate cysts) with a usually normal-sized uterus. Thus patient 1 has adenomyosis and patient 2 has endometriosis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Confluent glands without intervening stroma is the histologic hallmark of endometrioid carcinoma, not either of these benign conditions.
explanation_incorrect.B: Unopposed estrogen drives endometrial hyperplasia/carcinoma; adenomyosis and endometriosis are not defined by estrogen-driven gland proliferation or high malignant potential.
explanation_incorrect.D: The assignments are reversed: tissue within the myometrium is adenomyosis, while extra-uterine implants are endometriosis.
explanation_incorrect.E: Polymicrobial postpartum infection after cesarean delivery causes endometritis, not adenomyosis or endometriosis.

educationalObjective: Distinguish adenomyosis (endometrium within myometrium, boggy enlarged uterus) from endometriosis (endometrium outside uterus, powder-burn lesions and chocolate cysts).
